best_narrative.headline: Hims: California Telehealth Competitors Intensify Federal Lobbying on Prescribing Rules
best_narrative.body: Hims operates across consumer weight loss, sexual health, and general telehealth with material exposure to state asynchronous prescribing rules and compounded GLP-1 supply chain regulation, creating distinct regulatory complexity versus single-category peers. Four rival GLP-1 weight-loss telehealth prescribers filed federal lobbying disclosures on telehealth topics in the past 60 days, signaling coordinated effort to shape interstate prescribing standards before state legislatures act unilaterally. The most recent 10-K names state asynchronous prescribing rules, pharmacy compounding regulations, and GLP-1 compounded availability as material risks. This competitor mobilization typically precedes state-level regulatory clustering in top markets like California, New York, and Florida.

The most recent 10-K names state professional licensure variance and Medicaid reimbursement policy as material risks; competitive federal lobbying activity on telehealth topics signals potential moves to reshape licensing or reimbursement frameworks. Two mental health telehealth competitors filed federal lobbying disclosures on telehealth topics in April 2026, indicating coordinated policy engagement that may affect California, New York, and Texas operations where Teladoc holds significant contracted volume. The regulatory affairs lead should assess whether competing operators are mobilizing around specific state licensure or plan-reimbursement changes that could compress Teladoc's contracted margins or restrict cross-border prescribing workflows.

Your 10-K names state professional licensure variance and Medicaid reimbursement as material risks; given Teladoc's enterprise plan contracts across California, New York, and Texas, understanding the substance of these competing lobbying positions is operationally time-sensitive. best_narrative.body: Included Health operates as an enterprise virtual care platform contracted directly with health plans and employers, creating dependency on sustained Medicaid reimbursement and state licensure alignment across top markets including California, New York, and Texas. Industry-standard regulatory exposures for this business model include state professional licensure enforcement, cross-border telehealth practice restrictions, and Medicaid rate compression tied to in-state delivery mandates. Two direct competitors filed federal lobbying disclosures in April 2026 focused on telehealth scope and reimbursement, signaling organized industry positioning ahead of potential state-level licensing tightening or rate reviews. Your government affairs team should assess whether California's telehealth licensing board is preparing guidance changes that could affect contract renewals with health plans.

This often precedes state licensing board activity or health plan contract renegotiations tied to reimbursement and practice scope. Given Included Health's reliance on Medicaid and cross-state licensure alignment in California, New York, and Texas, a 15-minute call Thursday would help map which state regulatory moves pose contract or margin risk. Best,
[Rep Name]
